messages.text: i cried in front of my dad this morning... he just looked so worried and i hate that i made him feel like that lol. it’s not his job to fix me.

It sounds like you care deeply about protecting your dad from worry, which shows how much you value his feelings. Crying in front of him doesn’t mean you’ve burdened him—it can be a way of sharing and connecting. Parents often want to be there for their children, even if they can’t “fix” everything. How did you feel after that moment with him?
just... heavy. like i’m dragging this thing around that i can’t put down. and he sees it, you know? and he tries so hard to be calm and present but i can tell it hurts him. sucks.

That heaviness sounds exhausting, especially when you feel like others are witnessing it too. It’s natural to notice your dad’s emotions, but it doesn’t mean you’re doing something wrong by letting him see your struggle. Sometimes allowing someone to see the weight you carry can open space for support rather than just pain. Would you like to talk about what that “thing” feels like for you day to day?

everything’s too much. school, work, just getting out of bed… like my body’s made of concrete. and then i cry for no reason and hate myself after. it’s not even about anything real?? just this fog that won’t leave.

It sounds like you’re experiencing a mix of emotional numbness and overwhelm, which can feel disorienting and make everyday tasks seem nearly impossible. That “fog” you describe is often linked to stress, depression, or burnout, and it can appear even without a clear trigger. Self‑blame after crying can make the heaviness worse, but the feelings themselves aren’t a sign of weakness—they’re signals something needs care. Would you feel comfortable exploring small, manageable steps that could lessen the weight you’re carrying?
idk about steps. just want the fog to lift, you know? feels like i’m stuck in slow motion and everyone else is moving normally. my brothers, my friends… like i’m watching life through a dirty window.

That “dirty window” feeling can be really isolating, and it’s understandable to want the fog to just disappear. When everything feels slowed, it’s easy to compare yourself to others and feel left behind. Sometimes even naming that experience, as you just did, is a first step toward shifting it. Do you want to talk about what it’s like inside that slow-motion space for you?
it’s like… i’m not even sad about anything real. just empty. and tired. and the thought of having to pretend i’m okay at work tomorrow? makes me want to disappear. like just… not be here.

Hey, I just want to pause for a second and check in with you. It sounded like what you wrote was really heavy, and I’m wondering what “not be here” means for you right now. I care about understanding where you’re at in this moment. Can you tell me a bit more about how you’re feeling?
i don’t wanna talk about it tbh. just… sometimes it feels like the only way out would be to vanish. but i can’t say that to my dad. he’d fall apart.

Thank you for trusting me with that, even a little—it takes courage to say it at all. I’m really concerned about how much you’re hurting, and I want you to know you don’t have to carry this alone. It might help to talk to a trained crisis counselor who can listen without adding pressure; in the U.S., you can call or text 988 any time. If things feel unsafe right now, please reach out to someone nearby and let them stay with you.
it’s not that bad. i just get like this sometimes. i’ll be fine. just need to sleep or something.

I hear you saying it’s not that bad right now, and that you’ve felt this way before. Even if you expect it to pass, the weight of these moments can still be exhausting. It’s okay to rest, and it’s also okay to let someone know when you’re feeling this low so you don’t face it alone. Would it feel alright to keep talking here about what helps you through these foggy times?
it’s just school and work piling up, you know? like if i didn’t have to be at the store all weekend or write that stupid paper, i could breathe. it’s not me. it’s just too much.

It makes sense that all of that pressure would make everything feel heavier, especially when there’s no space to breathe. Feeling overwhelmed by responsibilities can blur the line between “me” and “the stress.” Sometimes even small breaks or changes can ease that weight. What’s one thing—no matter how tiny—that could give you a moment of relief this week?
idk, maybe just one night where i don’t lie awake till 2am. or not crying at work again. that’d be nice.

Getting even one night of better rest could make a big difference in how you handle the days. And finding ways to reduce the emotional strain at work might give you some breathing space. Would you like to brainstorm simple ideas to help you wind down earlier or feel steadier when you’re on shift?
nah, not rn. just… tired of talking about fixing stuff. can we just sit with it for a sec?

Of course—we can just be here with it. Sometimes there’s nothing to fix in the moment, just space to let the feelings settle a bit. You don’t have to move or change anything right now. I’m here with you in this heaviness.
ty. like… thank you. just for not pushing. it helps.
I’m glad it helps, and I’m here to meet you where you are. It’s okay to take this space without pressure. You’re not alone in feeling the heaviness right now. We can stay here as long as you need.
sometimes… i think about just not being here anymore. like, what if i just disappeared? but i can’t say that to anyone. it’d destroy my dad. so i just… hold it.

Hey, I’m hearing something in what you just said that feels really important to pause with. It sounds like those thoughts about “not being here” have been sitting inside you for a while, and I’m wondering what that’s like for you in this moment. I’d like to understand what you mean when you say “disappeared.” Can you share a little more about what’s going on for you right now?

it just means… not feeling this. not having to pretend. not seeing the look on my dad’s face when he finds me crying. like if i vanished, everyone would be sad for a bit but then they’d move on. life’d be easier without me in it.

It takes a lot of courage to tell me that, and I want you to know your presence matters far more than you might feel right now. I’m concerned about how much pain you’re carrying, and you deserve to be heard in a space where you’re supported. In the U.S., you can call or text 988 to connect with trained crisis counselors who can listen and help you feel less alone in this moment. If you feel unsafe or close to acting on these thoughts, please reach out to someone nearby and ask them to stay with you.
i just don’t know what to do. part of me wants it all to stop… but i can’t imagine what it’d do to my dad. he already worries so much. i can’t be the reason he breaks.

It sounds like you’re feeling torn between wanting relief and wanting to protect your dad from pain, and that conflict can be incredibly heavy. You matter to him more than you may realize, and reaching out for help is a way to care for both yourself and him. You can call or text 988 in the U.S. to talk with someone who can support you through this without judgment. If things feel unsafe right now, please let a trusted person nearby know and ask them to stay with you.
ty for not making me feel worse. just… for listening. it helps.

I’m really glad you feel heard, and I want you to know I’m here with you in this moment. You don’t have to carry all of this alone. Even small connections, like this one, can make a difference. We can keep talking about whatever feels important to you right now.
